items.title: Mercury is liquid for the same reason gold is yellow
items.claim: Mercury (Z=80) is the only metal liquid at room temperature, melting at -39°C. Cadmium just above it melts at 321°C; gold just before it at 1064°C. Mercury's anomaly is, like gold's colour, a consequence of special relativity.
items.prompt: What causes mercury's low melting point?

options.text: Relativistic contraction of mercury's 6s orbital makes its outer electrons less available for metallic bonding, so metallic bonds between Hg atoms are weak — much weaker than in cadmium or zinc

items.reveal:
Mercury has a filled 4f, 5d and 6s subshell. Relativistic contraction pulls the 6s electrons tightly to the nucleus, making them behave more like a noble-gas core than valence electrons.

Metallic bonding relies on delocalised valence electrons forming a 'sea'. With mercury's 6s electrons less willing to delocalise, the lattice is held together more by van der Waals forces and weak metallic interaction — like a giant noble gas.

Without relativistic effects, calculations suggest mercury would melt around 80°C, just like cadmium. The 'special' behaviour of an entire familiar element comes from one of physics' deepest theories.
items.why: Chemistry students treat elements as static atomic-orbital pictures. Heavy elements need relativity to be understood at all.

items.title: Aluminium 'should' fizz in water — why does it sit on the kitchen worktop?
items.claim: Aluminium is above iron, zinc and tin in the reactivity series. By the textbook, it should corrode rapidly. Yet aluminium foil, cans, ladders and aircraft hulls last for years.
items.prompt: Why is aluminium so unreactive in practice?

options.text: Pure aluminium does not react with oxygen
Aluminium reacts instantly with air to form a coherent, impermeable 4-nanometre layer of Al2O3 that protects the metal beneath; the reactive metal is locked behind its own oxide
Aluminium is coated with plastic at the factory
The reactivity series is wrong about aluminium

items.reveal:
Aluminium oxide forms in milliseconds when fresh aluminium meets air. Unlike iron oxide, Al2O3 has nearly the same molar volume as the metal it formed from (Pilling-Bedworth ratio about 1.3). The result is a tight, adherent film that excludes further oxygen.

Scratch the surface and a new film forms instantly. Dissolve the film in strong alkali (NaOH) or amalgamate the surface with mercury and the bare metal reacts violently — aluminium powder mixed with iron oxide is thermite, used for welding rails.

Anodising — deliberately growing a thicker oxide film electrochemically — gives extra protection and a surface that can hold dyes.
items.why: Reactivity series describes thermodynamic tendency. Passivation is the kinetic gatekeeper that decides whether reactions actually happen.

items.title: The conjugate base of a strong acid is essentially useless as a base
items.claim: HCl is a strong acid — it gives up its proton completely in water. The conjugate base Cl- has so little tendency to grab a proton back that it is functionally inert as a base. The same logic holds for HNO3 and NO3-, HClO4 and ClO4-.
items.prompt: Why does strength of acid translate to weakness of conjugate base?

options.text: If HA → H+ + A- is very far to the right (strong acid), then the reverse A- + H+ → HA has a very small equilibrium constant — A- doesn't reclaim protons. Ka and Kb of a conjugate pair multiply to Kw
Strong acids destroy their conjugate base on dissociation
Conjugate bases of strong acids are uncharged

items.reveal:
For any conjugate acid-base pair in water at 25°C: Ka × Kb = Kw = 10 to the minus 14.

HCl has Ka about 10 to the 7 (huge). So Cl-'s Kb is about 10 to the minus 21 — essentially zero basicity. Stir NaCl in water and the chloride doesn't appreciably grab protons. The solution stays neutral.

Conversely, the conjugate of a weak acid is itself a measurable base. CH3COOH has Ka 1.8 × 10 to the minus 5; CH3COO- has Kb 5.6 × 10 to the minus 10 — small but non-zero. So sodium ethanoate in water gives a slightly basic solution.

This reciprocal relationship is why salts can be acidic, neutral or basic depending on which conjugate is dominant.
items.why: Conjugate pairs are treated as labels. They are inversely related quantitatively, and that determines the chemistry of every salt solution.
